subject: Archaeology
title: The Trowel: An Archaeologist's Best Friend
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Trowel: An Archaeologist's Best Friend.

hook.text: The most important tool in archaeology costs about $15 — a four-inch pointing trowel made by Marshalltown.

buildup.text: Archaeologists scrape soil in thin layers with the trowel's flat edge, feeling for changes in texture and hardness.

discovery.text: An experienced digger can feel the difference between a natural deposit and a filled-in pit just by trowel pressure.

twist.text: Worn-down trowels are badges of honor. Some archaeologists are buried with theirs.

climax.text: Despite drones, lasers, and satellites, the hand trowel has not been replaced. No machine can match a trained hand.

punchline.text: A $15 trowel outperforms satellites when precision matters most.

quiz.question: Why hasn't the hand trowel been replaced by modern technology?
options: Budget constraints prevent most digs from using advanced equipment
No machine can match a trained hand at detecting subtle soil changes
Regulations require all excavation to be done with traditional tools
